proof_bridge.title: Real heights keep extended-real convexity precise
proof_bridge.summary: These are the library proof routes for the selected definitions, domain and indicator consequences, Theorem 2.4 and Examples 2.5–2.6. Orabona cites Rockafellar for Theorem 2.4 and leaves the norm example as an exercise.

steps.title: Project the epigraph to the effective domain
steps.detail: Every value below positive infinity has a real upper bound, even when the value is negative infinity. Lift two domain points to real epigraph heights. Convexity combines these lifts; the resulting finite height witnesses domain membership.
steps.fallback: Domain points admit real epigraph heights; their convex combinations do too.

steps.title: Use real values only where finiteness is proved
steps.detail: For Theorem 2.4, the no-negative-infinity hypothesis and domain membership prove that each value is finite. Convexity of the effective domain proves this also for the interpolated point. The real epigraph equivalence then translates the ordinary convexity inequality in both directions. Infinite values are never globally identified with zero.
steps.fallback: Under no-bottom and a convex effective domain, the strict-weight inequality is equivalent to epigraph convexity.

steps.title: Read constraints as epigraph intersections
steps.detail: The indicator epigraph is the product of the feasible set and nonnegative real heights. Adding an indicator intersects the original epigraph with the feasible cylinder; the no-bottom assumption excludes ambiguous infinite addition. Convexity follows from products and intersections of convex sets.
steps.fallback: Indicator convexity is equivalent to convexity of V; adding it restricts the epigraph to V.

steps.title: Check the affine and norm examples
steps.detail: Affine evaluation preserves convex combinations exactly. For the norm, apply the triangle inequality followed by nonnegative homogeneity. The real-valued coercion bridge transfers these inequalities into the same extended-real epigraph definition.
steps.fallback: Affine functions satisfy equality; the norm satisfies the convexity inequality.

steps.title: Separate finite loss from the below-top domain
steps.detail: Inside V the indicator is zero. Outside V it is top: adding bottom gives bottom, and adding a finite value or top gives top, never a finite real. Thus a finite constrained value requires both feasibility and a finite original value. The separate domain identity excludes bottom globally, so outside V the sum is top.
steps.math: \(f(x)+\iota_V(x)\in\mathbb R\iff x\in V\ \land\ f(x)\in\mathbb R;\qquad f> -\infty\Rightarrow\operatorname{dom}(f+\iota_V)=\operatorname{dom}f\cap V.\)
steps.fallback: Finite values exclude both infinities; the below-top domain excludes only positive infinity.

proof_bridge.title: From a local finite representation to every comparator
proof_bridge.summary: Theorem 2.7 is attributed to Rockafellar in the source. The implementation supplies a local finite-value bridge and a line-segment derivative argument, then treats an infinite comparator separately.

steps.title: Recover the function near the interior point
steps.detail: At x in the ambient interior of the effective domain, a whole neighborhood has values below positive infinity. Together with the global no-bottom assumption, these values are finite. Let iota denote the embedding from real to extended-real values. The embedded canonical real representative agrees with f locally, which gives the intended meaning to differentiability at x.
steps.fallback: The real representative agrees with f near x, after embedding into the extended reals.

steps.title: Compare the derivative with a secant slope
steps.detail: For a comparator y in the effective domain, restrict the convex real representative to the segment x+t(y-x). Its derivative at zero is the gradient inner product. Convexity bounds this derivative by the secant slope from zero to one.
steps.fallback: The directional derivative is at most the secant slope to a finite comparator.

steps.title: Restore extended-real values and include outside points
steps.detail: Rearrange the secant inequality and embed the finite values back into EReal. If y is outside the effective domain, f(y) is positive infinity, so the same lower bound is automatic. This split preserves the source quantifier over every ambient comparator.
steps.fallback: The supporting-gradient inequality holds for all y, including those with f(y)=positive infinity.

proof_bridge.title: Produce the expectation bound in two cases
proof_bridge.summary: These are the retained library steps for the displayed source inequality. The input has genuine finite Lebesgue coordinate means, represented by Bochner integrability in finite dimension. The inspected source prints no Jensen proof or extended-expectation well-definedness argument; the library steps below supply those obligations.

steps.title: Produce a finite negative part
steps.detail: Probability mass one and almost-sure domain membership give a nonempty-domain witness. Apply the global affine-minorant theorem to obtain a(X)+b, integrable because X is integrable. Its negative part bounds the negative loss part, proving the latter finite.
steps.fallback: The proof derives finite negative part; it is not an additional premise.

steps.title: Separate the positive-infinite case
steps.detail: If the positive loss integral is infinite, the finite negative part makes the signed expectation positive infinity. The desired inequality then follows from the top element. This branch does not separately assert finite expected loss.
steps.fallback: Infinite positive loss is allowed after controlling the negative part.

steps.title: Prove integrability in the finite case
steps.detail: Otherwise set Y=toReal(f(X)). Measurability and almost-sure domain membership, together with no bottom, give an exact finite embedding almost everywhere. The finite positive and negative part integrals make their maxima integrable; subtracting them proves Y integrable.
steps.fallback: Loss integrability is obtained inside this case, rather than assumed globally.

steps.title: Take the mean in the original epigraph
steps.detail: The integrable pair (X,Y) lies almost surely in the convex real-height epigraph. The finite-dimensional barycenter theorem places its mean in that same possibly nonclosed epigraph. The pair-integral identity and signed-real compatibility identify the resulting height with the expected loss.
steps.math: \((\mathbb EX,\mathbb EY)\in\operatorname{epi}_{\mathbb R}f\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(\mathbb EX)\le\mathbb EY=S_\mu(f\circ X).\)
steps.fallback: Actual epigraph membership gives the finite-case inequality.
